bib.title: Two-Level Meta-Rubrics for Evaluating Open-Ended Generation: GAMUT, a Benchmark for Factual Completeness

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Two-Level Meta-Rubrics for Evaluating Open-Ended Generation: GAMUT, a Benchmark for Factual Completeness". Xilun Chen, Zhaleh Feizollahi, Ross Goodwin, Seungwhan Moon, Scott Yih, Pinar Donmez, Babak Damavandi, Luna Dong, all Meta AI. arXiv 2607.19322v2 [cs.CL], dated Aug 6 2026 on the cover and 5 Aug 2026 in the arXiv stamp. Preprint, no venue. Data: huggingface.co/datasets/facebook/GAMUT. Code: github.com/facebookresearch/GAMUT.

COVERAGE: All 124,766 chars were extracted and I read them all (main text 0-56k, references skimmed, appendix A prompts, B examples, C annotator training). Appendix prompts A.1-A.4 and A.6 were read only in part (prompt boilerplate). Appendix B example figures come out as fragmented text. No extraction faults. I read the full note 04-graders.md and the headings and grep hits of 05-llm-as-judge.md, not all of 05.

NOTE FIT
- Best fit: 04-graders.md, section "Combining graders: scoring design", at the "Veto items" subsection, which holds Li's 4 rubric rules and the HealthBench paragraph. A second hook is "Binary vs. scales".
- The note already covers these ideas: binary over scales; self-contained rubric items; Essential/Important/Optional/Pitfall tiers with veto; HealthBench signed weights and one-criterion-per-call; all-pass false alarms (SPADE); report dimensions beside any composite.
- The note lacks these:
  1. Authoring a structured rubric and compiling it by fixed rules into flat binary checks.
  2. How to grade open-ended sets (a "mention at least N of" threshold check, with per-item credit that neither helps nor hurts for off-list answers) and ordering (a sequence check).
  3. A four-way verdict (meets, partially meets, missing, contradicts) with contradiction penalised above omission.
- 05-llm-as-judge.md "Decompose hard criteria" (line 169, completeness) is a secondary home for the "judge only flat binary checks" point. The scoring formula and compile rules belong in 04. It also sharpens the claim in 04 that a hallucination veto is separate from quality.

CORE CLAIM: Rubric authoring needs structure (open sets, order, importance). Judges are more reliable on flat binary checks than on rich structure. So author a structured meta-rubric, then mechanically compile it to a flat binary checklist for the judge. GAMUT instantiates this as a factual-completeness benchmark.

CLAIMS (ranked)
1. The compile rules are deterministic. Flexible list: a threshold check plus per-item credit one tier lower if the pool has 7 or fewer items, else coverage thresholds. Process: a presence check per step plus a sequence check. Strict list: one check per item.
 number: none
 setup: per-question rubric, Section 3.2
 quote: "A flexible list becomes two kinds of check: one or two baseline thresholds and additional credit for broader coverage." and "naming two clears the requirement, naming more raises the Valuable score, and naming a dish outside the seven neither helps nor hurts."
 where: Sec 3.2, p5
2. Scoring formula: s = (M + λP + μC) / (M + P + S + |μ|C), λ=0.5, μ=-2, tier weights 0.6/0.3/0.1 (Answer-Critical / Valuable / Context). A contradiction counts as more than one check in the denominator, so a cautious answer outranks a confidently wrong one. The weights are global so that many minor Context checks cannot drown out a few Answer-Critical ones. An empty tier has its weight redistributed.
 number: λ=0.5, μ=-2, w=0.6/0.3/0.1, score range -1 to 1
 quote: "Because µ enters both numerator and denominator, a contradiction both removes credit and counts as more than one check, so a cautious answer outranks a confident but wrong one. We useλ = 0.5 andµ=−2."
 where: Sec 3.3, p6. The values are not tuned or sensitivity-tested.
3. Structure is pervasive in the questions.
 number: 98% of 1,813 questions have at least one structured component beyond Simple Knowledge. Flexible list 86%, strict list 49%, process 17%, relationship 6%. Meta-insight in 13% (295). Mean 15.2 checks per question (median 15, max 41), split 5.9/5.8/3.5 across the tiers. 97% of meta-rubric items and 94% of compiled checks cite a web snippet. About 10 snippets per rubric, over 9,400 distinct pages.
 setup: GAMUT, n=1,813
 quote: "For 98% ofGamut's questions a flat rubric of independent, individually required checks would be wrong"
 where: Sec 6.2-6.3, p10-12. This is a count of structures, not a test that flat rubrics grade worse.
4. Headline benchmark result.
 number: best Gamut score 58.7% (Gemini 3.1 Pro); worst 5.1% (Llama 3.2 11B). Claude Opus 4.8 53.1, GPT-5.4 42.6, Claude Sonnet 4.6 41.5, GPT-4o 34.2, Qwen3-VL 235B 33.0. The best model meets 55.2% of elements, with 29.2% missing and 4.1% contradicts.
 setup: 14 models, 1,813 multimodal questions, one judge (Gemini 3.1 Pro), one run, no confidence intervals
 quote: "the strongest (Gemini 3.1 Pro) reaching aGamutscore of only 58.7%" (Sec 1, p3). Table 1: "Gemini 3.1 Pro 58.7 63.9 51.9 45.1 55.2 11.5 29.2 4.1"
 where: Table 1, p8
5. Omission dominates error.
 number: missing verdicts are 68.3% for Llama 3.2 11B and 29.2% for Gemini 3.1 Pro. Contradiction rate is 11.5% for Qwen3-VL 8B and 2.6% for Claude Opus 4.8.
 quote: "the dominant failure is omission rather than error:missingverdicts account for roughly two-thirds of the rubric elements for the weakest models and over a quarter even for the strongest"
 where: Sec 5.1, p8
6. Judge robustness (the only judge-reliability evidence).
 number: Gemini and Claude Opus 4.8 judges give an identical ranking, with per-model scores within 1.8 points. Self-score gaps are within 0.3 points. Qwen3-VL 235B as judge is more lenient by 4 to 11 points with "only adjacent swaps".
 setup: the same 14 models, 1,813 questions, same rubrics, 3 judges, one run each
 quote: "Gemini and Claude produce an identical ranking, with per-model scores within 1.8 points of each other, and neither favors its own answers: each scores itself within 0.3 points of how the other scores it"
 where: Sec 5.1 and Table 2, p8-9
7. Text-only variant.
 number: removing the image raises the score by about 10 to 20 points, e.g. Gemini 3.1 Pro 58.7 to 73.7 (+15.0), GPT-4o +22.3, Claude Opus 4.8 +6.8
 setup: 1,806 questions (7 dropped as still image-dependent), same judge
 quote: "removing the image raises theGamutscore by roughly 10 to 20 points for nearly every model"
 where: Sec 5.2 and Table 3, p9-10
8. Construction process and human involvement.
 number: 1,938 images from CRAG-MM, 1,843 questions, 12 hand corrections, 1,813 final. Questions are reviewed by 2 annotators plus a third adjudicator. Rubric refinement is one LLM round, because "a second refinement round changed little". Annotators pass gold jobs at 95% and a rubric quiz at 90%, with 10% audits.
 quote: "The refined rubrics are revised by a small in-house team working closely with the authors, since a general annotation pool could not improve on the LLM-generated rubrics"
 where: Sec 4.2, p7 and App C, p29

LIMITS
Stated or implied by the authors:
- Single benchmark, everyday topics, English.
- The authors claim the recipe is general ("applies to rubric-based evaluation of open-ended generation more broadly") but test only factual completeness.
Unstated:
- The central premise, that judges "are far more reliable on flat, binary checks than on rich structure", is not tested. There is no flat vs structured ablation, no human-vs-judge agreement (no kappa, no per-check accuracy), no repeat-run variance, and no inter-annotator agreement on rubric edits. The judge-robustness evidence is cross-judge ranking agreement only, and the three judges could share the same errors.
- Gemini 3.1 Pro generated the questions and rubrics, refines them, acts as the primary judge, and ranks first. The judge prompt tells it to "evaluate holistically, not mechanistically", which sits oddly with the "mechanical" framing. Human verification mitigates the first part but does not measure it.
- λ, μ and the tier weights are chosen by fiat with no sensitivity analysis. No confidence intervals or seeds.
- Rubric coverage is capped by what the annotators and web search found, so "missing" may partly reflect an incomplete rubric. The answer is credited for off-list valid items only through thresholds.
- A rubric with about 15 checks may reward long answers. No length analysis is reported.
- The headline "highly discriminative" is supported only by agreement with expectations ("newer and larger models outscore older"), which is circular, not a measured discrimination statistic.

INTERNAL INCONSISTENCIES
- "No judge favors its own answers" holds for Gemini and Claude only. Qwen3-VL 235B as judge scores itself 44.0 against 33.0 (Gemini) and 31.2 (Claude), a +11.0 shift. GPT-4o, just above it, moves only +4.6 (34.2 to 38.8). Under the Qwen judge Qwen3-VL 235B (44.0) overtakes GPT-4o (38.8) and Qwen3-VL 8B (23.0) overtakes Llama 4 Scout (18.6). That looks like self-preference and is not the same as leniency.
- The paper says the text-only ordering is "broadly preserved". In Table 3 Claude Opus 4.8 (59.9) falls below Gemini 2.5 Pro (66.2), Gemini 3 Flash and Claude Opus 4.6 (62.1), and GPT-4o (56.5) nearly matches GPT-5.4 (58.5).
- "10 to 20 points" is approximate: Opus 4.8 is +6.8 and Qwen3-VL 8B +9.7.
- The Table 3 multimodal column equals Table 1 to the decimal although it is said to cover 1,806 rather than 1,813 questions, so the scores were probably not recomputed on the subset.
- "Claude Opus the lowest" contradiction rate (about 3%): true for Opus 4.8 (2.6%), but Opus 4.6 has 5.2% and GPT-4o 3.4%.
- 1,938 images but "one question per image" gives 1,843, so 95 images are unaccounted for.

BUILDS ON (as printed)
- Decompose-search-verify precision metrics: FActScore (Min et al., 2023), VeriScore (Song et al., 2024).
- Recall and reference-fact methods: VeriFact (Liu et al., 2025), FACTORY (Chen et al., 2025).
- Rubric and checklist judging: G-Eval (Liu et al., 2023), Prometheus (Kim et al., 2024), FLASK (Ye et al., 2024), CheckEval (Lee et al., 2025), Autorubric (Rao and Callison-Burch, 2026), HealthBench (Arora et al., 2025), ExpertLongBench (Ruan et al., 2025).
- Closest benchmark: FACTS Multimodal (Cheng et al., 2025; Jacovi et al., 2025), which has an essential/non-essential split.
- Images from CRAG-MM (Wang et al., 2025).
- Related deep-research benchmarks: MMDeepResearch-Bench, MiroEval.

CODE: no code is given. The judge prompt (App A.5) is worth keeping. It sets a system role of "rigorous and objective evaluator" and asks for "evaluate holistically, not mechanistically". It has four verdicts with worked rounding and specificity examples: "269 cu in" vs "around 270" is meets; "between 250 and 300" is partially_meets; "340" is contradicts. "contradicts -- use ONLY for substantive factual errors". Location: p23-24.

FIGURES (figures.py not run; captions are in the extracted text)
- Fig 1, p2: the jollof rice example showing the meta-rubric (A Simple, B Strict List, C Flexible List with meta-insight, D Process) beside the compiled checklist grouped by tier. This is the best figure candidate. It explains the compile step faster than prose and could be redrawn for the note.
- Fig 3, p11: rubric statistics, a panel on how common each structure type is. Lower priority.
- Fig 2: topic composition per domain. Not useful for the course.
- Fig 4 and 5, App B: full worked examples.

PROBLEMS: no embedded instructions found in the PDF. Figures and the App B examples extract as fragmented text. Wide-table columns were read from the extraction and cross-checked (verdicts sum to 100). The paper's dates (2026) are consistent with the target note's currency.
